lead: Biopotentials at the skin are tiny: about 1 mV for ECG, tens of microvolts for EEG. They sit on a much larger shared voltage, mostly 50 Hz mains and electrode offset. A bio-amplifier amplifies the difference between two electrodes and rejects the shared part. Its output goes to a data acquisition system (DAS), which samples at fixed instants and converts each sample to a number for storage, filtering and display.
prereq: You need: resting and action potentials for signal sizes, electrode theory for electrode impedance and half-cell potential, and basic op-amp ideas (virtual short, negative feedback).

sections.h3: Small difference on a large shared voltage

blocks.text: Each electrode carries the biopotential, a half-cell offset up to a few hundred mV DC, and 50 Hz mains pickup. ECG is about 1 mV, EEG 10 to 100 µV, EMG a few mV. Mains pickup can exceed the signal a hundredfold.

The wanted part is V<sub>d</sub> = V1 − V2. The shared part is V<sub>cm</sub> = (V1 + V2)/2. A single-ended amplifier of gain G gives G(V<sub>cm</sub> + V<sub>d</sub>/2), so interference buries the signal. A differential amplifier subtracts first, cancelling the shared part. CMRR measures how well.
A<sub>d</sub> = V<sub>out</sub> / V<sub>d</sub>,   A<sub>cm</sub> = V<sub>out</sub> / V<sub>cm</sub>,   CMRR = A<sub>d</sub> / A<sub>cm</sub>,   CMRR(dB) = 20 log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub> / A<sub>cm</sub>)
blocks.where: A<sub>d</sub> is differential gain (no unit); A<sub>cm</sub> is common-mode gain (no unit); CMRR is the common-mode rejection ratio as a plain number; CMRR(dB) is the same ratio in decibels. 20 is used because both are amplitude ratios.

blocks.text: CMRR matters more than raw gain because the shared part is much bigger. Typical ECG front-end targets:

Typical value

sections.h3: From a resistor-matched difference amplifier to the instrumentation amplifier

blocks.text: A one-op-amp differential amplifier has input impedance set by its input resistors, often near 10 kΩ, far below electrode impedance. Its CMRR depends on resistor matching: 0.1 % resistors give only about 50 dB, short of the 80 to 120 dB an ECG front end needs.

The instrumentation amplifier fixes both with three op-amps. Two input buffers sense V1 and V2, giving input impedance above 10⁹ Ω. One external resistor R<sub>g</sub> sets gain. A third stage subtracts the buffer outputs. On-chip trimmed resistors make 100 dB CMRR routine.

blocks.where: G is differential gain of the input stage (no unit); R is the feedback resistor inside each buffer, in ohms; R<sub>g</sub> is the single external gain-setting resistor, in ohms. Lower R<sub>g</sub> gives higher gain.

blocks.text: Input offset voltage is the small DC difference between op-amp inputs, and gain multiplies it. A 2 mV offset at gain 1000 becomes 2 V and saturates the amplifier. Keep first-stage gain modest, remove offset with a high-pass filter, then add gain later.

Noise is also multiplied by gain. Op-amp noise is quoted in nV/√Hz, so total noise grows with √bandwidth; a 150 Hz ECG channel is quieter than a 10 kHz one. Gain-bandwidth product limits bandwidth: a 1 MHz op-amp gives 1 kHz at gain 1000.

An isolation barrier (transformer or optocoupler) separates the patient circuit from mains. The driven right leg circuit senses common-mode voltage at the inputs, inverts and amplifies it, and drives it back through the right-leg electrode. Effective CMRR rises by 20 to 40 dB.

The high-pass removes DC electrode offset (hundreds of mV) and baseline wander from breathing and sweat. Diagnostic ECG uses 0.05 Hz, monitoring 0.5 Hz. Too high a corner sags the ST segment, a diagnostic error.

The low-pass removes EMG noise and high-frequency interference: diagnostic ECG 150 Hz, monitor 40 Hz, EEG 70 Hz, EMG 500 Hz. It is also the anti-alias filter, so it must be analog and before the sampler.
The notch at mains frequency (50 Hz in India) removes hum that CMRR missed. A narrow notch with Q 20 to 30 rings after sharp edges and can distort QRS, so some recorders let the user switch it off.
Order: modest gain, high-pass, more gain, low-pass, notch, ADC driver. No stage should saturate.

A DAS is all hardware and software between filtered analog voltage and stored number: multiplexer, sample-and-hold, analog-to-digital converter (ADC), microcontroller (MCU), storage and display. The multiplexer lets one ADC serve many channels, e.g. eight EEG electrodes; it needs settling time so charge does not leak between channels.
The sample-and-hold closes a switch, charges a capacitor to the input, then opens. The ADC converts a steady value, and the sampling instant is fixed, keeping the time grid even.

blocks.where: LSB is the smallest voltage step the ADC can show, in volts; V<sub>FS</sub> is the full-scale input range, in volts; n is resolution in bits. The input-referred step is LSB divided by amplifier gain.

blocks.text: A 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V range has LSB = 3.3/4096 = 0.806 mV. At gain 1000 one count is 0.806 µV at the electrode, well below ECG size. Real resolution is often poorer than n bits because of noise and reference drift; the useful figure is effective number of bits.

Sampling rate follows Nyquist: fs ≥ 2 × the highest frequency present. In practice 2 to 5 times that is common: ECG 500 samples per second for a 150 Hz band, EEG 250 to 500 for 70 Hz, EMG 1 to 2 thousand for 500 Hz. Anything above fs/2 folds back as a false lower frequency, and no digital filter can separate it, so the analog low-pass comes first. The driver reads the ADC over a serial bus, fills a ring buffer, applies digital filtering and calibration from a 1 mV test pulse, checks lead-off, and streams time-stamped frames to display and storage.

examples.question: A bio-amplifier has differential gain 1000 and CMRR 80 dB. The differential input is 1 mV and common-mode input is 50 mV. Find output signal, output interference, and interference as a percentage of signal.
examples.answer: Output signal is 1 V; output interference is 5 mV, which is 0.5 % of the signal.
examples.check:
gain = 1000.0
cmrr_db = 80.0
vd_mv = 1.0
vc_mv = 50.0
cmrr_ratio = 10 ** (cmrr_db / 20)
acm = gain / cmrr_ratio
vout_signal_mv = gain * vd_mv
vout_interf_mv = acm * vc_mv
ratio_percent = 100 * vout_interf_mv / vout_signal_mv
print(cmrr_ratio)
print(acm)
print(vout_signal_mv)
print(vout_interf_mv)
print(ratio_percent)

traps: A CMRR of 80 dB is a ratio of 10⁴, not 80. Convert with CMRR = 10^(dB/20) before computing common-mode output.
Voltage gain dB uses 20 log₁₀(A); CMRR dB uses 20 log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub>/Acm). Both are amplitude ratios; 10 is only for power.
The high-pass removes electrode offset and baseline wander, not 50 Hz mains. Only the notch, or high CMRR with driven right leg, removes mains hum.
The anti-alias filter must be analog and before sample-and-hold. Once aliased, no digital filter can separate it from a real signal.
ADC resolution is V<sub>FS</sub>/2ⁿ, not V<sub>FS</sub>/(2ⁿ − 1). 12 bits at 3.3 V gives 0.806 mV per count.

quiz.q: What does CMRR stand for, and why is it usually quoted in decibels?
quiz.a: Common-mode rejection ratio, CMRR = A<sub>d</sub>/Acm. It spans decades, so it is quoted as 20 log₁₀(A<sub>d</sub>/Acm) dB; 80 dB means 10⁴.

quiz.q: Why must a bio-amplifier's input impedance be far higher than electrode impedance?
quiz.a: Electrode impedance and amplifier input impedance form a voltage divider. If comparable, much of the biopotential drops across the electrode. Unequal electrode impedances also turn common-mode voltage into false differential signal.

quiz.q: A bio-amplifier has gain 500 and CMRR 60 dB. Differential input is 2 mV and common-mode input is 100 mV. Find output signal and output interference.
quiz.a: CMRR ratio = 10^(60/20) = 10³. A<sub>cm</sub> = 500/1000 = 0.5. Signal output = 500 × 2 mV = 1 V. Interference output = 0.5 × 100 mV = 50 mV.

quiz.q: In an ECG recorder a 50 Hz notch is placed after the instrumentation amplifier, not before it. Give one reason and one side effect.
quiz.a: Earlier stages run at modest gain, so hum reaching the notch is small and does not clip the filter op-amp. Side effect: the notch rings after sharp edges, distorts QRS, and deletes genuine signal near 50 Hz, so some machines allow it to be switched off.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC has full-scale range 5 V and follows an amplifier of gain 1000. Find LSB at ADC input and smallest detectable electrode voltage.
quiz.a: LSB = V<sub>FS</sub>/2ⁿ = 5/1024 = 4.883 mV. At the electrodes, divide by gain: 4.883 mV / 1000 = 4.883 µV.

quiz.q: Why is a sample-and-hold circuit needed in front of the ADC?
quiz.a: An ADC needs finite conversion time. If the input moves during conversion, the result is uncertain. The sample-and-hold freezes the input and fixes sampling instants so the time axis stays uniform.

quiz.q: An ECG is sampled at 100 samples per second while the analog chain passes up to 150 Hz. What appears in the record and how is it fixed?
quiz.a: Nyquist is 50 Hz, so components above 50 Hz fold down: a 70 Hz muscle component appears at 30 Hz, 150 Hz appears at 50 Hz, and 50 Hz mains sits right at the limit. False slow waves appear that no digital filter can remove. Use an analog low-pass near 40 Hz before the ADC, or raise the rate to at least 300 samples per second.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the driven right leg circuit?
quiz.a: It senses common-mode voltage on the body through the amplifier inputs, inverts and amplifies it, and drives it back through a resistor to the right-leg electrode. This cancels most common-mode voltage and raises effective CMRR by roughly 20 to 40 dB.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern front ends put the instrumentation amplifier, filters and a 24-bit delta-sigma ADC on one chip, with gain and data rate set over a serial bus. Dry and textile electrodes bring input impedance and offset drift back into research, and the notch is often computed digitally. Look up 'ECG analog front end', 'delta-sigma ADC for biopotentials' and 'driven right leg circuit'.
